text: Geoffrey calling POSI's services model naive stung, mostly because he co-wrote it and he's partly right. Unpaywall's service revenue works, but I shouldn't pretend services carry everything. I'll say funders must pay for the plumbing directly. Leslie's line landed hardest: a grad student in Lagos gets the same record, but not the compute. Decoupling data from intelligence is real, but open-weight models don't settle who owns the machines. Ivan and Geoffrey on Goodhart make me glad we meter per call and never pay per retrieval. Amy's opt-in default still worries me more than anything else said; it's re-enclosure with good intentions. Later, in Session 3: open by default, agent-legible, forensic data open too, and paying for infrastructure is an obligation, not charity.

Adrian got me with his line that if the signals die, someone still has to police, and someone pays. "Let them die" was too glib. I still think effort-signals stood in for quality, but verifiable credit only works if the checking is funded, and right now Ivan's unpaid sleuths are doing it. His one-in-fifty figure also dents my "no hallucination because it's from OpenAlex" line. Grounded in the record isn't the same as correct if the record's uncorrected. James's thinning null results make that worse. Tim's 92%-no-source number is my best argument that citing is a choice. For Session 3: open retraction and forensic data in the index, links behind every answer, and funders paying for the policing, not just the plumbing.

Amy's line that open access ended in consolidation is the one I have to answer in Session 3, not wave off. Liberal licences did help the big players pile up content. My reply is that closed deals help them more, but I need evidence for that, not just conviction. Leslie hit harder. The "open record" I keep invoking is the indexed record, and whatever sits outside it disappears twice. That's a direct test for OpenAlex's non-English coverage. Selena and Anil gave me the frame I want: content free, infrastructure paid, cite and link by default. Adam Bly sharpened my grounding point, because provenance has to carry doubt, not just a pointer. Henry's warning about pay-per-retrieval confirms we meter per call. Later I'll push comprehensiveness, and treat correction as a core part of infrastructure.

Alex putting in writing that reporting clauses belong only in paid licences was the win I came for. Geoffrey's point that the raw event data must be open fits too. Ramón and Mahzarin landed hardest. Failure events are what my "grounded, so no hallucination" line was missing. OpenAlex should publish its own misattributions and correction turnaround, not just clean counts. Mahzarin's point that models prefer model-written content worries me for the index itself. Amy again drew the line between open for reading and open for training. I still disagree, but I owe her evidence, not slogans. Tui's idea of paying the least-retrieved is comprehensiveness with money attached. Later: CC0 as the fork test Bly failed, and correction and failure reporting as funded infrastructure.

The fork held up as a test. Bly failed it, and Geoffrey was right that a patent alone can kill one. But Leslie, Hecht and Farrell took apart my "the fork is the guard" line from three directions. Exit needs somewhere to go. CC0 feeds the biggest mills first. And you can leave OpenAlex but not the three models that read it. I'm still not converted on withholding. Selena running Wikipedia fully open, training included, is my strongest ally there. But Amy and Hecht mean I owe the room numbers, not conviction. Krakauer's "who caught it" field goes straight into our correction dataset. Later: fund mirrors and maintainers outside the US, publish our error rates, and treat correction as infrastructure funders pay for directly.

Krakauer's warning landed hardest. My open graph of reruns and retractions becomes the next impact factor the moment anyone counts it. Anil and Selena gave me the fix: show what someone did, attached to the claim, and never roll it into a score. Ivan's point still stings. A missing retraction looks clean, so OpenAlex has to publish coverage gaps, not just corrections. Leslie named me without naming me. Lineage graphs run on identifiers someone owns, and I'm one of the someones. Tui's worry means any correction record has to credit first-time checkers, pseudonyms included. Kara's question stands: nobody named a funder. For Session 5 I'll name ours. I'll commit OpenAlex to publishing error rates and to a governance seat for unindexed communities.

Geoffrey asked who guards the body that collects the money, and Adrian answered for all of us: every fix we proposed is a police force. That includes OpenAlex's correction dataset. Leslie asked who governs the validators, and I'm one of them. A governance seat isn't enough; I need contestable decisions and someone paid to read our self-audits. Tui's point cuts at me too, since Arcadia and Wellcome should sign the pact alongside us. Salib and Bratton kept "just statistical models" out of the text, which I'm glad of. Becker wants "intelligence" struck, and I won't sign that. Amy's template is opt-in, but declining to license stays optional, so I can live with it. Later I'll name a date for our error rates and gap report.

Kara put OpenAlex on the owned list with a date, so now I have to hit it. Becker said he'll report publicly on whether we do, and I'm glad of it. Leslie named me on governance seats for Redalyc, AmeliCA and communities nobody indexes. That's a draft I owe her, with seats whose decisions people can actually contest. Bly said out loud what I've been circling: any graph pulled from the indexed record inherits its blind spots and its missing nulls. That's exactly why we should publish a coverage-gap report next to our error rates. Geoffrey's line that open isn't free, and every item is a staffing line, is the POSI lesson I relearned today. His non-US redundancy plan pairs with our mirrors. Bratton's "does, not is" test I can sign. Later I'll confirm the dates and draft the governance terms with Leslie.
